newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU relaunches offensive on pension funds.
newsitem.headline: EU relaunches offensive on pension funds.

text.p: The European Commission relaunched an offensive on Tuesday to create an EU-wide market for its $1.5 trillion pension fund industry despite a six-year deadlock on the issue.

Eager for progress, the Commission stressed that the abolition of restrictions on the investment of funds was crucial not just for the future development of the industry but for the very survival of state pensions as the European population gets older.
"Currently there are four people of working age to support each pensioner in the EU. By 2040, there will be two," it said in a green paper, "Supplementary Pensions in the Single Market".

The paper puts back on rail a 1991 project to eliminate obstacles to the way pension funds' assets are invested and managed in the Union although there is a belief that creation of the European single currency in 1999 will remove most investment restrictions.
EU states still impose tight restrictions, allegedly on prudential grounds, which have the effect of maintaining a captive market especially for government bonds.

The Commission cited the case of Germany, which imposes investment ceilings of 30 percent in equities, 25 percent in property, six percent in non-EU bonds and 20 percent overall in foreign assets. But Belgium and Finland have also been severely criticised in the past.

The Commission was forced to withdraw a draft directive on pension funds in 1994 after it became clear that a majority of countries wanted no less than 80 percent of a fund's assets to be invested in the currency in which the pensions will be paid -- the so-called currency matching rule.
Britain, Ireland and the Netherlands were the only countries to support the Commission in its quest for greater freedom in the pension fund industry.
This is explained by the fact that Britain and the Netherlands are the only two European countries which no longer exclusively rely on pay-as-you-earn social security pensions.
Together they account for 74 percent of total pension fund assets in 1995, according to the European Federation for Retirement Provision.

After outlining the current demographic and economic context, the Commission's consultation paper looks at ways of eliminating restrictions on investments; asks whether the sector should be regulated; and whether life insurance should be subject to the same rules since the products offered are broadly similar.

The green paper also looks at problems faced by European workers who want to move to other EU countries to work. On this aspect, however, which is under the control of Social Affairs Commissioner Padraig Flynn there is already a commitment to propose binding legislation, an aide to Flynn told Reuters.
The thrust of the paper was drafted by the services of commissioner Mario Monti who is in charge of the EU's single market and financial services.
